grammar.title: Structure
grammar.unavailable: Structural analysis is not available for this language yet.
grammar.disclaimer: Rule-based analysis. Roles marked with ? are uncertain.

verbSecond.title: Verb in second position
verbSecond.body: In German main clauses the conjugated verb occupies the second position; the first position can hold the subject, an adverb or an object.

verbFinal.title: Verb at the end after “{{subordinator}}”
verbFinal.body: Subordinating conjunctions send the conjugated verb to the end of their clause.

relativeClause.title: Relative clause
relativeClause.body: The relative pronoun takes gender and number from the noun it refers to, and its case from its role inside the relative clause. The verb goes to the end.

passive.title: Passive voice (werden + participle)
passive.body: “werden” with a past participle forms the passive: the action is in focus, not who performs it.

perfect.title: Perfect tense with “{{auxiliary}}”
perfect.body: The auxiliary is conjugated in second position and the participle closes the clause (verbal bracket). Verbs of movement or change of state use “sein”.

future.title: Future with “werden”
future.body: “werden” plus an infinitive at the end of the clause expresses the future or a supposition.

modal.title: Modal verb “{{modal}}”
modal.body: Modal verbs are conjugated in second position and send the main verb, as an infinitive, to the end of the clause.

twoWayPreposition.title: Two-way preposition “{{preposition}}”
twoWayPreposition.body: Accusative for movement towards a destination (where to?), dative for location (where?).

prepositionCase.title: “{{preposition}}” takes the {{case}}
prepositionCase.body: This preposition always governs the same case, which determines the article ending.

adjectiveDeclension.title: Adjective declension: {{declension}} ({{ending}})
adjectiveDeclension.body: After definite articles adjectives take weak endings; after ein-words mixed endings; without an article strong endings that show the case.

case_nom.title: Nominative (“{{article}}”)
case_nom.body: The nominative marks the subject: who or what performs the action.

case_acc.title: Accusative (“{{article}}”)
case_acc.body: The accusative usually marks the direct object, and follows prepositions such as für, durch, ohne.

case_dat.title: Dative (“{{article}}”)
case_dat.body: The dative usually marks the indirect object (to whom?) and follows prepositions such as mit, nach, bei, von.

case_gen.title: Genitive (“{{article}}”)
case_gen.body: The genitive expresses possession or follows prepositions such as wegen and während.

caseAmbiguous.title: “{{article}}” could be {{cases}}
caseAmbiguous.body: Without knowing the noun's gender and number with certainty, the article alone does not determine the case.

konjunktiv2.title: Konjunktiv II: “{{form}}”
konjunktiv2.body: Used for unreal or hypothetical situations, wishes and polite requests.

konjunktiv1.title: Konjunktiv I: “{{form}}”
konjunktiv1.body: Mostly used in reported speech, typical of news and formal writing.

modalParticle.title: Possible modal particle: “{{particle}}”
modalParticle.body: Modal particles add tone (surprise, emphasis, softening) rather than lexical meaning. Their translation depends on context.

verbAfterClause.title: Verb first after the subordinate clause
verbAfterClause.body: The fronted subordinate clause occupies the first position of the sentence, so the conjugated verb of the main clause comes right after it, still in second position overall.

expressionNotes.separable: A separable verb: in main clauses the prefix goes to the end of the clause, while the conjugated stem stays in second position.
expressionNotes.reflexive: Used with a reflexive pronoun that agrees with the subject (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch).
expressionNotes.prepositionalObject: The object is introduced by a fixed preposition, which determines its case.
